title: Misinformation Persists in Complementary Health: Evaluating the Reliability and Quality of YouTube-Based Information on the Use of Acupuncture for Chronic Pain
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content appraisal of the 54 top-viewed English-language YouTube videos on acupuncture for chronic pain. It reports a share of items coded misleading with an explicit inaccuracy-based case definition (14.8%, n = 8 of 54), which meets the CONTENT criterion. It additionally reports shares of videos below the mDISCERN and GQS cut-offs, which are instrument-based QUALITY shares and are recorded as QUALITY rows (excluded from prevalence).

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language videos only. Authors note this 'limits the relevance or generalizability of this study to countries outside the United States'
estimates.date: Not reported; manuscript received 13 January 2024, accepted 6 April 2024, published 16 April 2024
estimates.measure_type: % of top-viewed YouTube videos on acupuncture for chronic pain classified as misleading
estimates.denominator: 54 YouTube videos on acupuncture for chronic pain, drawn from the top 200 by view count over three search queries and retained if >1 minute, English audio or subtitles, >7000 views, acupuncture-related and not duplicates
estimates.definition: A video was 'misleading' if it had 1) an inaccurate definition of acupuncture; 2) at least one inaccurate statement about the pain-reducing mechanism of acupuncture; or 3) at least one inaccurate statement about the indications, adverse effects, benefits, and potential outcomes of acupuncture. Judged by two independent reviewers against criteria from a prior systematic review of acupuncture randomised trials, with a third reviewer resolving discrepancies.
estimates.misinfo_def: "The criteria for a video to be deemed misleading were 1) inaccurate definition of acupuncture; 2) at least one inaccurate statement about the pain-reducing mechanism of acupuncture; or 3) at least one inaccurate statement about the indications, adverse effects, benefits, and potential outcomes of acupuncture."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 54 videos, 57.4% were categorized as useful, 14.8% were misleading, and 27.8% were neither.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results (p.1509); repeated in Results p.1512 and Table 1 p.1514
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers (S.K. and H.T.) coded each video useful / misleading / neither using criteria from a previous systematic review identifying evidence-based uses for acupuncture (Madsen et al., BMJ 2009); any discrepancies were resolved by a third reviewer (R.S.D.). Inter-rater reliability is reported for the two instrument scores only - mDISCERN Cohen's kappa 0.74 (95% CI 0.58-0.89, 83.3% agreement) and GQS kappa 0.44 (95% CI 0.24-0.62, 61.1% agreement); NO kappa is reported for the useful/misleading/neither classification that produced this value.
estimates.moderator_quote: Several search term combinations were used to query the YouTube platform (www.youtube.com): "acupuncture for chronic pain", "acupuncture pain relief", "acupuncture pain". ... The top 200 videos by view count were initially selected after the first query. ... After reviewing videos for relevance and removing those that met exclusion criteria, a final list of the top 54 videos by view count were selected to be included in the final analysis.
estimates.notes: Construct call: the useful/misleading/neither scheme is a usefulness typology, which the instructions would normally send to QUALITY, BUT the 'misleading' arm is defined purely by the presence of an INACCURATE statement judged against an external evidence base (a systematic review of acupuncture trials), so a wholly accurate video cannot receive the label. That makes it explicit falsity coding and therefore CONTENT rather than QUALITY. Denominator is a rank-truncated most-viewed set on a single health topic, hence denom_scope topical + denom_selection curated. No data-collection date is reported anywhere in the paper; year coded as the publication year 2024 (search must predate the 13 January 2024 submission). No country is stated for the content; coded Global because YouTube search results are not localised in the report, with the authors' own English-only caveat noted.

estimates.measure_type: % of videos scoring below 3 on the modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) reliability instrument, i.e. low reliability
estimates.denominator: The same 54 top-viewed English-language YouTube videos on acupuncture for chronic pain
estimates.definition: Score below 3 on the 5-question modified DISCERN scale (clear aims; reliable sources used; balanced and unbiased; additional sources listed; areas of uncertainty mentioned), one point per 'yes'. 'A score greater than 3 indicated high reliability.'
estimates.misinfo_def: Not a misinformation definition: mDISCERN measures the reliability of presentation, not the truth of the content.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers (S.K. and H.T.) scored each video on mDISCERN; discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer (R.S.D.). Cohen's kappa 0.74 (95% CI 0.58-0.89), 83.3% agreement - substantial.
estimates.moderator_quote: The reliability of the information presented in the videos was assessed using the 5-question scoring system called mDISCERN, which was adapted from the longer 15-question DISCERN scale. ... A score greater than 3 indicated high reliability.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, to be excluded from prevalence pooling: mDISCERN is an instrument score, and a wholly accurate video can score low on it (e.g. for not listing additional sources). Kept because the instructions ask that instrument-based shares be recorded as QUALITY rather than dropped.

estimates.measure_type: % of videos scoring below 3 on the Global Quality Scale (GQS), i.e. low quality
estimates.denominator: The same 54 top-viewed English-language YouTube videos on acupuncture for chronic pain
estimates.definition: Score of 1 or 2 on the 5-point Global Quality Scale (1 = poor quality, most information missing; 5 = excellent quality and flow), classified by the authors as low quality.
estimates.misinfo_def: Not a misinformation definition: GQS measures overall usefulness and flow for patients, not the truth of the content.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers (S.K. and H.T.) scored each video on the GQS; discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer (R.S.D.). Cohen's kappa 0.44 (95% CI 0.24-0.62), 61.1% agreement - only moderate, the weakest reliability statistic in the paper.
estimates.moderator_quote: The videos as a whole were scored between 1 and 5, where a score of 1 or 2 was classified as low quality, a score of 3 was intermediate quality, and a score of 4 or 5 was good quality.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, excluded from prevalence pooling. Confidence medium rather than high only because the GQS inter-rater agreement is weak (kappa 0.44, 61.1% agreement), so the cut-off share is unstable; the count itself (7 of 54) is stated verbatim in Table 3.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and NOT extracted: (1) 57.4% (n = 31) useful and 27.8% (n = 15) neither useful nor misleading - the complements of the misleading share, not misinformation numerators, and R8 forbids keeping computed complements; they are quoted inside the CONTENT row's source_quote for transparency. (2) The production-source composition figures - 41.8% (n = 13) of useful videos from healthcare institutions, 0% of misleading videos from healthcare institutions, 87.5% (n = 7) of misleading videos from health media vs 25.8% (n = 8) of useful videos, 80% (n = 12) of 'neither' videos from health media - these are shares of a source type computed WITHIN a usefulness category; they say nothing about the prevalence of misinformation and are not within_misinfo_content falsity shares either. (3) Mean mDISCERN and GQS scores by category (useful 3.48/3.77, neither 2.73/2.87, misleading 2.38/2.50) - scale means with no share, no row per the instructions. (4) Externally cited figures that R8 forbids keeping: 'more than 40% of the healthcare seeking population uses social media platforms, such as YouTube, as a source for medical information', '70% of patients with low back pain tried out at least one CHA, while over 40% used at least two', '1 in 5 adults in the United States experience chronic pain', and YouTube's '122 million daily active users'. The one judgement an adjudicator should look at is the CONTENT-vs-QUALITY call on the 14.8% misleading share, argued in that row's notes.

rob.design: Cross-sectional appraisal of publicly available YouTube videos (Mayo Clinic IRB exempt). Three search queries ('acupuncture for chronic pain', 'acupuncture pain relief', 'acupuncture pain'); results filtered by the platform relevance algorithm then sorted by view count; top 200 screened, 54 retained (>1 minute, English audio or subtitles, >7000 views, acupuncture-related, non-duplicate, has audio). Two independent reviewers extracted video metadata, classified production source into six categories, coded usefulness against criteria from a prior systematic review, and scored mDISCERN and GQS; a third reviewer adjudicated all discrepancies. Reliability: mDISCERN kappa 0.74 (83.3% agreement), GQS kappa 0.44 (61.1% agreement); no reliability statistic for the usefulness classification. Comparisons by t-test and chi-square in GraphPad Prism 9. Data-collection date not reported; view-count threshold (>7000) and English-only restriction acknowledged by the authors as limitations.

rob.item10_quote: Out of the final list of 54 videos, 57.4% (n = 31) were categorized as useful, while 14.8% (n = 8) were designated misleading, and 27.8% (n = 15) were neither useful nor misleading.
